newsitem.title: CROATIA: Tudjman wins another five years to reform Croatia.
newsitem.headline: Tudjman wins another five years to reform Croatia.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman has returned to power aware of the need to spread the country's wealth more evenly and temper western suspicions of his authoritarian rule.

Incomplete returns showed Tudjman won around 60 percent of a low turnout in Sunday's presidential elections, riding his popularity as the leader of Croatian independence to crush two rivals, including a former communist.

But the 75-year-old president has consistently shown himself to be more popular than his ruling HDZ party, which many Croats believe has exploited the post-communist era to seize an unfair share of power and prosperity for its members.

He now has two more years to restructure the economy and restore fallen living standards before parliamentary elections at which HDZ authority is likely to face stronger opposition than Tudjman personally.
Tudjman, who guided Croatia through four years of war after its 1991 secession from former Yugoslavia, acknowledged popular resentment after his victory, telling reporters:
"We are leaving behind the state of war. Now we shall dedicate ourselves, with all our forces, to raising standards of living for the entire population."
Although Tudjman has won his first peacetime endorsement, the after-effects of the war are still strongly visible and not only in the economy.
The West wants more evidence that democracy and media freedom is taking root before allowing Croatia closer integration with the European Union.
A diplomat in Zagreb said it would be "well into the next century" before Croatia would be considered for membership, though negotiations on a trade and cooperation agreement are expected this year.
Tudjman is under U.S. and EU pressure to ease the return to their homes of Croatian Serb refugees whose rebellion was blamed by Croatians for the outbreak of the war for independence.

While the West regards Tudjman as a realist, uncertainty about Croatia's future is compounded by his failure to appoint an heir apparent, despite medical reports from the United States that he has stomach cancer.
One of his first tasks will be to manage the return to rule by Zagreb of Eastern Slavonia, the last Serb enclave in Croatia, from United Nations administration.
Due to expire next month, the U.N. mandate may be prolonged but Tudjman has made it clear he wants to take control in July.
Thousands of Croatians who fled eastern Slavonia under Serb assault in 1991 will want to return to their homes, now inhabited by Serbs.
Those Serbs are meant to return to their pre-war homes in other parts of Croatia but some who did were beaten and their houses were burned down.
Tudjman won praise from the U.N. for assuring Serb leaders Zagreb would create conditions for the co-existence of Croats and Serbs to try and heal the wounds of war.
Yet some diplomats say it is too early to expect everything to go quite as smoothly as the West wants.
"There's a visceral feeling about the return of Serbs which is not going to improve very quickly," one said.
"I think we are asking too much. We are less than two years from the conflict. Is it reasonable, is it realistic, to expect people to bury their differences and say it was all a mistake?"

Vesna Popovski at the School of Slavonic and East European Studies in London said the hardliners brought in by Tudjman when he rose to power after creating the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) in 1990 were not interested in joining the West.
Another problem Tudjman will face is how to make the Croat community in Bosnia support the Moslem-Croat federation, a cornerstone of the Dayton peace treaty that ended the war.

He garnered the support and money of hardline Croat emigres in 1989 when he formed the HDZ and has rewarded some with high political positions. But America is determined he should reduce their influence and force them to comply with the Federation if it is to support Croatia's integration with the West.

One diplomat said: "There is always a danger Croatia might find itself in isolation but that is not in the clear interests of the country. I take it Tudjman knows where his interests are...he always proved to be a rational man in the end."
